cases.title: EO 14110 outside assessment
cases.drafterAgreement: Agree with drafter and sheet option 6a.

firstReport.locator: Comparison, policy-level government capability assessment; JSON item 67 / us-eo14110:Q06

cases.criterion: Requires or provides for assessment of the model or developer practices by someone other than the developer. Partly covers permitted/empowered assessment or assessment of filings/documents.
cases.locator: Sec. 4.4(a)(i)(A)-(B), 88 FR 75200-75201; GovInfo Federal Register HTML.
cases.answer: Change my first report’s final partly reading to not-found; agree with the drafter (6a). Freshly retrieved the official GovInfo Federal Register HTML of EO 14110, section 4.4(a)(i)(A)–(B), including the page break at 75200–75201. It mandates a government threat study, consultation to evaluate model capabilities, and a report assessing types of models and recommending oversight. That is relevant context, but it does not establish an outside-assessment requirement for a covered developer’s model or practices. My earlier partly answer stretched the question’s object from the model to a general policy inquiry; neither of Q06’s written partly cases supplies that extension. Record this passage as read and set aside. This classification does not deny that the order directs government evaluation work.

cases.title: BIS 2025 on U08
cases.recommendedReading: articulation of second limb only, qualified; option 7b
cases.drafterAgreement: Disagree with context-only 7a under the existing second limb; agree the agents perform compliance work.

firstReport.locator: Part A1 comparison, item 8; comparison with same-family audit, U08

cases.criterion: Agent-initiated transactions would use/require/favour programmable or tokenised money, stablecoins or tokenised deposits, OR AI would interact with those forms of money in ways that matter for the monetary system.
cases.locator: The promise of tokenisation > Tokenisation and next-generation correspondent banking, closing paragraph before Box C; preceding platform paragraphs and Box B read.
cases.answer: Narrow my first reading; retain 7b for U08’s second limb only. Freshly retrieved BIS’s official HTML of Annual Economic Report 2025 chapter III, dated 29 June 2025, and read the correspondent-banking section plus Box B. The text places AI-agent compliance reporting in a proposed platform joining tokenised central-bank and commercial-bank money, with efficiency and integrity as stated system functions. That is a specific interaction relevant to the proposed monetary infrastructure, rather than relevance inferred merely from the chapter title. However, the conjunction does not establish that AI agents themselves perform the embedded pre-screening checks or initiate payments. Box B’s copilots qualify the role; they do not remove it. No stablecoin preference or realised deployment is established. Context-only requires narrowing or clarifying the existing second limb, as option 7c proposes.

cases.criterion: AI agents acting for people or firms will/could initiate, negotiate or execute payments and transactions, changing payments or payment-system demands.
cases.locator: The Next Frontier of Payments Innovation, 29 September 2025; paragraph beginning Let’s turn from DLT to AI, preceding payment-efficiency question and following compliance example.
cases.answer: Hold my final first-report reading: context/bears-on, not an articulation of U07; agree with the sheet’s current recommendation 15a. Freshly retrieved the Federal Reserve Board’s official HTML of Waller’s speech, dated and delivered 29 September 2025, and reread the payments-efficiency paragraph with its surrounding discussion. It says agents execute tasks for people or companies; it does not identify those tasks as initiating, negotiating or executing payments or transactions. The immediate cross-border example is compliance automation, which can improve payments without delegating the payment itself. The broader speech discusses settlement through DLT, but does not assign that action to AI agents. My blind search’s provisional Waller candidate was already narrowed in the first report’s passage comparison. Removing its earliest-articulation role does not decide the separate relay-eligibility question in decision 6.

cases.scopeReading: Yes: section 5, pp. 3-4, defines frontier developers by training or initiating training of such models. The compute count includes original training and subsequent fine-tuning, reinforcement learning or other material modifications. Large frontier developers additionally exceed $500 million prior-year aggregate gross revenue with affiliates. General-purpose capability alone is not the trigger.
cases.dutiesReading: Sections 10(c), 15 and 20 impose transparency-report, incident-report and whistleblower duties on frontier developers; section 10(a), (d) adds framework and annual independent-audit duties for large frontier developers. Section 18 separately starts large-developer disclosure duties on 1 January 2027. These are enacted future duties, not evidence of compliance or duties already in force on the check date.
